slides.sub: It's a phrase. And it's why you think you have things you never bought.
Open your declarations page. The words are not there. Nobody at the carrier uses them either.
Liability. Comprehensive. Collision. Uninsured motorist. Rental. Each one is a line you either bought or you didn't.
Liability + comprehensive + collision. That's it. It leaves out rental, uninsured motorist and medical.
If a coverage isn't listed with a limit next to it, you don't have it.

piezas.caption:
"Full coverage" isn't a product. It's a phrase people use for liability + comprehensive + collision — and it leaves out the coverages that matter most when something goes wrong.

Pull up your declarations page. If a coverage isn't listed with a limit next to it, you don't have it.

Save this for the next time someone tells you they're "fully covered."

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

piezas.tema: Nadie elige un deducible, elige un precio

slides.sub: They choose a lower price. The deductible is what they gave up in exchange.
Higher deductible, lower premium. You saved a little every month and agreed to pay a lot on one bad day.
The savings look small each month. The gap shows up all at once, when you can least plan for it.

slides.titulo:
It only touches
your own car.
slides.sub: Comprehensive and collision. Liability has no deductible at all.
If you can't say your deductible from memory, you didn't choose it. You accepted it.

piezas.caption:
Most people don't pick a deductible. They pick a cheaper premium, and the deductible is what they traded away for it.

It only applies to damage to your own car — comprehensive and collision. Liability has no deductible.

Do you know yours without looking?

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

piezas.tema: Listar el carro en apps de alquiler

slides.titulo:
You listed
your car for rent.
slides.sub: Your personal policy may have stopped covering it the moment you did.
Renting your vehicle to others is excluded. So is any paid use of your car. Most policies carry both.

slides.titulo:
The platform's
plan is not your policy.
slides.sub: It covers what its terms say it covers, for as long as the rental period runs. Nothing before, nothing after.
On the highest-earning tier, the owner absorbs physical damage to their own vehicle.
Call your carrier and ask what happens if a renter crashes your car. Get the answer before you need it.

piezas.caption:
Renting out your own car on a car-sharing app can put you outside your personal auto policy — most contain an exclusion for vehicles rented to others, and another for any paid use.

The platform's own plan only covers what its terms say, during the rental. And on the highest-earning tier, the owner can absorb the damage.

Ask your carrier before you list, not after.

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

piezas.tema: La app de reparto y el periodo 1

slides.sub: Your personal policy may have stopped covering you right then.
App on, waiting. Heading to pick up. Passenger or order in the car. They are not covered the same way.
App on, no job assigned. Personal policy often excludes it. Platform coverage is at its thinnest.
Most carriers sell a rideshare or delivery add-on. It usually costs a few dollars a month.
Tell your agent you drive for an app and ask what covers you in period one.

piezas.caption:
Driving for a delivery or rideshare app splits your day into three periods, and they are not covered the same way.

Period 1 — app on, no job assigned — is where personal policies commonly exclude and platform coverage is thinnest.

Most carriers sell an endorsement that closes it, usually for a few dollars a month. Ask for it by name.

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

piezas.tema: El deducible no aplica a liability

slides.titulo:
At fault?
You don't pay
a deductible.
slides.sub: Not for the other driver's car. That's not how liability works.

slides.titulo:
Deductibles live
on your car only.
slides.sub: Comprehensive and collision. Those are the coverages that repair your vehicle.
Their car, their injuries. No deductible, up to your limit.
One coverage protects your car. The other protects everyone else from you.
Once you see it, the rest of the policy stops being confusing.

piezas.caption:
If you cause a crash, you don't pay a deductible for the other driver's car. Liability coverage has no deductible.

Deductibles only exist on the coverages that repair your own vehicle — comprehensive and collision.

One coverage protects your car. The other protects everyone else from you. That's the whole structure.

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

piezas.tema: Símbolos de autos cubiertos en póliza comercial

slides.titulo:
One digit decides
which vehicles
are covered.
slides.sub: It's on every commercial auto policy. Most owners have never looked at it.
The broadest. Owned, hired, borrowed — all of it.
If a vehicle isn't on the schedule, it isn't covered. Buy a truck and forget to add it, and you have nothing.
Hired autos. Non-owned autos — like your employee's own car, on your errand.

slides.titulo:
Go look at
your dec page.
slides.sub: The symbols sit next to each coverage. They decide everything else on the page.

piezas.caption:
Every commercial auto policy has a single digit that decides which vehicles the policy even applies to. Symbol 1 is any auto. Symbol 7 is only the vehicles listed on the schedule. Symbols 8 and 9 cover hired and non-owned autos.

A business on symbol 7 that sends an employee out in their own car has a gap it doesn't know about.

Check the symbols on your declarations page.

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

slides.titulo:
A deer is
comprehensive.
A tree is collision.
slides.sub: Same car. Same damage. Two different coverages.
You hit something, or something hits you. Applies even when the fault is yours.
Theft. Hail. Fire. Flood. Vandalism. Glass. Animals.
They're separate coverages, priced separately, and you can carry one without the other.
Check your dec page. They're listed on separate lines, with separate numbers.

piezas.caption:
Hit a deer, that's comprehensive. Hit a tree, that's collision. Same car, same damage, two different coverages with two different deductibles.

Collision is impact. Comprehensive is everything else that happens to your car — theft, hail, fire, flood, vandalism, glass, animals.

They're separate lines on your policy. You can carry one without the other.

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

slides.sub: Three numbers on your card that decide everything. The third one is the one that ruins people.
The most the policy pays for any one injured person.
The most it pays for everyone injured, in total. Two people hurt, and it splits.
The other driver's car. A modern vehicle can pass that number without trying.
The policy stops at its number. The rest doesn't disappear — it just isn't the carrier's anymore.

piezas.caption:
25/50/25 means $25,000 per injured person, $50,000 per accident, $25,000 for the other party's property.

The third number is the one that catches people. A modern vehicle can exceed $25,000 without much effort — and above the limit, the difference is yours.

Check your three numbers. Most people have never looked.

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

slides.titulo:
PIP pays
no matter
whose fault it was.
slides.sub: So does Med Pay. They are not the same thing.
Medical bills, and often lost wages and some services while you recover.
Medical bills only. Usually a smaller limit.
Some require PIP. Some offer Med Pay as an option. Some have neither.
It's on your dec page, and it's the coverage that pays first after a crash.

piezas.caption:
PIP and Med Pay both pay regardless of who caused the crash — but they're not the same coverage.

PIP is broader: medical bills plus, often, lost wages. Med Pay is medical bills only, usually with a smaller limit.

Which one you can even buy depends on your state. Check your declarations page.

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

piezas.tema: Rental reimbursement vs loss of use

slides.titulo:
Rental reimbursement
and loss of use
are not the same.
slides.sub: Buying the wrong one is why people end up paying for the rental car themselves.
A coverage you bought on your own policy. It has a daily cap and a total cap.
What the at-fault driver's carrier owes you while your car is being repaired.
Typical caps. If the shop takes six weeks and the rental costs more per day, the gap is yours.
It depends on who caused the crash. Ask before you drive off the rental lot.

piezas.caption:
Rental reimbursement is a coverage you buy on your own policy, with a daily cap and a total cap. Loss of use is what the at-fault driver's carrier owes you while your car is in the shop.

Different things, different payers. Which one applies depends on who caused the crash.

Ask before you drive off the rental lot.

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

slides.titulo:
The coverage
that pays when
they have nothing.
slides.sub: Uninsured and underinsured motorist. It's the first one people drop to save money.
They hit you and there's nothing behind them.
They carry the state minimum. Your bills are larger than their limit.
Plenty of drivers carry exactly the minimum their state requires. Nothing more.
It's the cheapest line on many policies, and the one that covers what you can't control.

piezas.caption:
Uninsured motorist pays when the driver who hit you has no policy. Underinsured pays when they have one, but their limit is smaller than your bills.

Plenty of drivers carry exactly the state minimum and nothing more. That's what UM/UIM is for.

It's often one of the cheapest lines on the policy — and the first one people cut.

Educational only. Not legal or insurance advice.

slides.titulo:
Someone decides
what your policy
pays.
slides.sub: That job is called a claims adjuster. Most people have never heard of it.
Reading the policy, applying it to what happened, and putting a number on it.
Every post here is the knowledge the job runs on. That's not a coincidence.

slides.titulo:
It's a career
with a door.
slides.sub: A license, some training, and a first assignment. No degree required in most states.
The path is in the link in bio.

piezas.caption:
After almost every crash in America, someone reads the policy and decides what it pays. That job is a claims adjuster.

The job is coverage knowledge — which is what every post on this account is.

If the work sounds interesting, the path to it is in the link in bio.
